subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 38-year-old man who has taken 4 g of vitamin C daily for 2 years to "boost his immune system" presents with sudden severe left flank pain radiating to the groin, nausea, and gross hematuria. Urinalysis shows many red blood cells and envelope-shaped crystals, and a noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen shows a 6-mm radiopaque stone at the left ureterovesical junction. Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels are normal.
question: Which of the following best explains the formation of this patient's kidney stone?

options.text: Ascorbic acid is metabolized to oxalate, and excess oxalate is excreted in the urine
Vitamin C is excreted unchanged and precipitates as a uric acid stone
High-dose vitamin C alkalinizes the urine and precipitates calcium phosphate
Vitamin C increases intestinal calcium absorption and produces hypercalcemia
Vitamin C forms a stone composed of cystine

explanation_correct: Excess vitamin C can cause calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis because oxalate is a metabolic product of ascorbic acid, and the extra oxalate precipitates with calcium in the urine. The envelope-shaped crystals and radiopaque stone are characteristic of calcium oxalate. Other features of vitamin C excess include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fatigue, and high doses can worsen iron overload by increasing dietary iron absorption.

explanation_incorrect.B: The stone is calcium oxalate rather than uric acid, and uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain radiography.
explanation_incorrect.C: Excess ascorbic acid does not cause calcium phosphate stones through urinary alkalinization; oxalate is the culprit.
explanation_incorrect.D: Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone are normal, and vitamin C does not produce hypercalcemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cystine stones occur in cystinuria and are radiopaque, but this patient's crystals and history point to calcium oxalate.

educationalObjective: High-dose vitamin C can cause calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis because ascorbic acid is metabolized to oxalate.
